analytic.title: Real-Time Scheduling of Reconfigurable Distributed Embedded Systems with Energy Harvesting Prediction

div.p: In this paper, we are interested in real-time scheduling of a distributed reconfigurable embedded system powered by a renewable energy source. Uncertainty of energy availability in energy harvesting systems makes the problem of task scheduling more challenging. A reconfiguration scenario is defined as an operation that allows the addition-removalmodification of tasks which may result in timing infeasibility. The system updates its behaviour in accordance with user requirements in reaction to unpredictable events from the environment. The contribution of this paper concerns energyaware strategies for adaptive task allocation. The proposed approach is decomposed into two phases a) Static task assignment heuristic, and b) Dynamic adjustment algorithm. In order to maintain schedulability and sustainability of the application software, the dynamic adjustment algorithm performs three functions: i) Migration, ii) Degradation of the execution mode, and iii) Removal of tasks. We employ a novel energy prediction algorithm. A simulation study brings to light the effectiveness of the proposed approach in terms of deadline success ratio.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Distributed architectures are widely used in embedded applications including biomedical, automotive, aircraft and industrial area. The correctness of these architectures depends not only upon their accurate results, but also upon the imposed deadlines in which the results are delivered [1]. Real-time systems are classified according to the consequences of missing deadlines as: (i) Hard real-time systems where the non respect of timing requirements may lead to severe consequences, (ii) Soft real-time systems where missing some deadlines may be tolerable [2].

Recently, reconfigurable computing system has become a subject of a great deal of research, due to its potential to satisfy the flexibility of software with the high performance of hardware [3]. Some academic and industrial research works have been made in recent years to develop reconfigurable control systems [4]. The occurrence of unpredictable events may involve reconfiguration of the system in terms of addition, removal or modification of parameters of tasks. Thereafter, some existing or added tasks may violate deadlines due to energy starvation or processing overload, for example.

The energy harvesting technology is a promising alternative to surmount energy limitation and finite life time of batteries. Several technologies are proposed for environmental energy harvesting, in particular solar and vibrational energies [5], [6]. In an energy harvesting-based system, the main issue is to guarantee that at any moment the system does not consume more energy than harvested and available in the storage. However, realizing such systems that meet energy requirements and application's performance may be nontrivial depending upon many factors. The uncertainty in the energy availability provided by free sources makes the developing of reliable and energy-efficient power-management solutions more challenging. Therefore, energy autonomy in networked reconfigurable embedded systems is a major concern. To tackle this problem, an efficient solution is to use energy management policies that dynamically consume the available energy according to real-time system states. To this end, the literature has revealed several approaches focusing on harvested-energy management that adapt the system to uncertainty in energy availability by deploying energy harvesting prediction algorithm [7]. However, none of prior works focusing on real-time scheduling in energy harvesting systems consider dynamic reconfiguration scenarios that may lead to deadline violation and/or energy starvation. Consequently, both static task assignment and dynamic adjustment in reconfigurable multiprocessor energy harvesting systems are new challenges that we address in the current paper.

In this paper, we address the scheduling issue in reconfigurable multiprocessor energy harvesting systems. We will contribute as follows. i) An appropriate energy prediction algorithm is proposed to increase the accuracy of our task allocation scheme, ii) We propose a novel task allocation algorithm for an energy harvesting distributed embedded system that operates in two phases: A static phase is executed offline and a dynamic one is executed online to adapt the system to unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios and to cope with fluctuating behaviour of the energy source, iii) We evaluate the performance of our proposed approach in terms of deadline miss ratio. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on energy harvesting aware task allocation for reconfigurable distributed embedded systems.

The remainder of the paper is as follows. Section II gives a brief state of the art about first energy aware scheduling, reconfigurable real-time systems, and finally energy harvesting predictions algorithm. Section III formalizes the system model and section IV presents the proposed energy harvesting predictions algorithm. Section V describes the proposed approach for real-time scheduling with energy harvesting predictions. Section VI reports simulation results that bring to light the effectiveness of these solutions measured in terms of deadline miss ratio. Finally we conclude in Section VII with a summary of the proposed contributions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: In this section, we present a state of the art about first, real-time scheduling under energy harvesting constraints, and second, distributed reconfigurable embedded systems. We also present an overview on prediction of renewable energy.

div.head: A. Real-Time Scheduling with Energy Harvesting Requirements
div.p: Although, several important works have focused on scheduling in uniprocessor energy harvesting based embedded systems [8], [9], energy harvesting aware scheduling for the multiprocessor case has received much less attention. Among the most interesting studies, the research work in [10] defines an efficient particular EDF scheduling algorithm named EH-EDF (Energy Harvesting-Earliest Deadline First) for aperiodic tasks, where decisions are taken at run-time without having prior knowledge about the future energy production and task characteristics. The research work in [11] defines an epoch-based approach for the energy management in performance constrained Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) that utilizes energy harvesting solutions. The proposed approach utilizes two energy management techniques: Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) and Dynamic Modulation Scaling (DMS). The authors of [12] propose an energy-efficient fault tolerance task allocation scheme for multiprocessor SoCs in real-time embedded energy harvesting systems. The proposed task allocation scheme achieves fault tolerance by first reserving enough slack on each processing element and second re-executing the faulty task whenever necessary. Nevertheless, none of these works consider the challenges arising from the uncertainty in the energy availability provided by ambient sources.

div.head: B. Reconfigurable Real-Time Systems
div.p: Interesting academic and industrial works focused on reconfigurable systems where automatic reconfigurations are applied by intelligent agents [13]. More recently, studies dealt with the same issues with low-power considerations. In [14], two combinatorial optimization approaches based on Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) processors are described for minimizing energy consumption. A mechanism adjusts deadlines so as to guarantee the feasibility conditions and overcome the problem of task rejection. In [15], a software-agent-based architecture provides four solutions to reconfigure the system at run-time. In addition, the agent provides three virtual processors in order to reduce the system's power consumption. However, no work deals with energy harvesting assumptions.

div.head: C. Harvested Energy Prediction Approaches
div.p: The authors of [7] propose a solar energy prediction model named exponentially weighted moving-average (EWMA) which is based on an exponentially weighted movingaverage filter [16]. This method relies on the assumption that the energy available at a given time of the day is similar to that available at the same time of previous days. However, EWMA leads to significant prediction errors when weather conditions are frequently changing i.e, when sunny and cloudy days are mixed. In order to address the shortcomings of EWMA, Piorno et at. propose in [17] the prediction method weather-conditioned moving average (WCMA). Proenergy identifies patterns (slot values) of typical days called sunny, cloudy, and rainy days as examples. Harvest predictions are generated by picking the pattern that has the closest match within a given comparison window. Other works have proposed methods based on machine learning as described in [18].

div.head: III. FORMALIZATION
div.p: This section gives a mathematical representation of a distributed reconfigurable real-time system under energy harvesting constraints. The system includes an harvester and an energy storage.

div.head: A. System Overview
div.p: Figure. 1 shows the overall structure of the system considered in this paper. The energy predictor algorithm predicts the availability of the harvested energy over an estimation interval I. Based on this estimation, the energy predictor builds the "execution windows" as depicted in Figure . 2. In fact, an execution window is defined as the time interval where the energy is assumed to be a constant over time. Hence, the estimation interval I is partitioned into a set of execution windows W = {w 1 , .., w r }. Each execution window w k , k ∈ {1, .., r}, is characterized by a length L w k , an energy rate, and a scheduling strategy. The idea of time-segmentation during run-time workload control is first proposed in [19]. The author proposes to divide time into identical length windows. However, in this paper we propose that the execution window's length is variable and it depends upon the profile of the harvested energy. Therefore, the scheduling algorithm will be able to cope with unpredictable fluctuation in energy availability and to unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios. The main objective is to guarantee that all critical tasks meet their deadlines, and to minimize the ratio of deadline missing for the non-critical tasks.

2) Energy Storage Model: In this paper, we consider a hybrid energy storage model (battery and super-capacitor). A storage unit is defined by B j = (E jmax , E jmin ), ∀j = {1, .., m}, where E jmax and E jmin are respectively the minimal and maximal energy that can be stored. Note that for simplicity and without loss of generality, we assume that the energy storage can be completely depleted to as little as zero. The energy available in the storage B j at a particular time t is denoted by E Bj (t). We also assume that each energy storage can be charged up to its capacity.

div.head: 3) Energy Consumption Model:
div.p: The processor P j supports only one operating frequency. Its energy consumption is only due to dynamic switching energy. Consequently, it consumes negligible energy in the idle state when it does not execute jobs. Therefore, we assume that the energy consumed by processor P j is equal to zero when it does not execute jobs (idle state). Furthermore, the energy consumed in [t 1 , t 2 ] is the cumulative amount of WCEC of tasks executed by processor P j between t 1 and t 2 . The energy consumed by a job in any unit time-slot is greater than or equal to the energy produced at the same unit time-slot.

div.head: D. Task Model
div.p: We assume that the system Sys performs two classes of tasks: i) A critical task set ψ c containing n tasks ψ c = {τ 1 , .., τ n }, and ii) A non-critical task set ψ nc containing m tasks ψ nc = {τ 1 , .., τ m }. Hence, if meeting a given task's deadline is critical to the system's operation, then the task's deadline is considered to be hard and the task is called critical. Whereas, if it is desirable to meet a task's deadline but occasionally missing the deadline can be tolerated, then the deadline is considered to be soft and the task is called non-critical. In this paper, we admit that the criticality doesn't necessarily mean short deadlines, we can consider then critical tasks with long deadlines. The software platform Γ contains a set ψ of N tasks ψ= {τ 1 , .., τ N } (N = n+m). Task τ i , i = {1, .., N }, is characterized by: i) Period T i . Tasks have implicit deadlines, i.e., deadlines are equal to periods, ii) Worst case execution time (WCET) C i in conformance with the classical task model of Liu and Layland [2], iii) Worst case energy consumption (WCEC) En i and iv) A degree of criticality dc i that defines its applicative importance. So, τ i is characterized by: {T i , D i , C i , En i , dc i }. In addition, a non critical task τ i is characterized by a (m i , k i ) parameter which indicates that we tolerate that at least m instances among k consecutive ones must respect their deadlines for task τ i . div.head: IV. PRE-ENERGY: SOLAR ENERGY PREDICTOR
div.p: We discuss a new energy prediction algorithm. The latter combines historical observations based on learning machines, local observations, and weather forecast in the purpose to derive more efficient and precise predictions on the future energy availability. The literature has revealed several works to predict the solar energy using machine learning techniques and environmental parameters. The Gaussian processes regression (GPR) has been proved more robust than other regression approaches. Therefore, our prediction model has its foundation on GPR [21]. For energy management and prediction, we consider a prediction interval I which is discretized into N equal duration time slots. In order to predict the future energy incoming E e (s, I) for a slot s on an interval I, the pre-energy algorithm combines two terms: i) The historical energy estimation E h (s, I), and ii) The current interval's elapsed slot energy estimation E e (s-1, I).
div.formula: E e (s, I) = (1 -α)E h (s, I) + αβE e (s -1, I)(9)
div.p: The parameter α shows the trade-off between these terms (0 α 1), and β for the different weather conditions (cloudy, sunny,...). The historical energy estimation E h (s, I) is calculated using the GPR.

div.head: V. REAL-TIME SCHEDULING WITH ENERGY PREDICTION
div.p: The task scheduling problem on a reconfigurable distributed real-time system is known to be NP-complete and considered as one of the most challenging problems in parallel computing [2]. This paper addresses the even more difficult problem of scheduling on systems constrained by both real-time and energy constraints with uncertainty on the energy availability. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic framework based on energy availability predictions. An important underlying idea in our framework is the partitioning of time into a set of execution windows. The length of the execution windows is a variable that depends on the availability of the energy in the future. Each execution window is characterized by a length, an energy rate, and a scheduling strategy. Due to the time-varying behaviour of the harvested energy, the actual harvested energy may not correspond to the predicted energy values. Therefore, in order to maintain schedulability of the application software and system sustainability, if the error margin is higher than some predefined thresholds, then the dynamic energy harvesting adjustment algorithm is executed. The main idea of our proposed approach is to compare at the beginning of each execution window the rate of the harvested energy A w k and the predicted value H w k . If the margin error exceeds some predefined thresholds E r , then the dynamic adjustment algorithm is executed.

div.head: A. Motivation
div.p: A run-time external reconfiguration scenario is a dynamic operation allowing the addition/removal of the critical and non-critical tasks. Thereafter, some tasks may miss their hard deadlines and the energy constraint may be violated. Further, each processor in the multiprocessor platform should satisfy the hard real-time constraint in which the CPU processor utilization is no greater than the schedulable utilization U x , in addition to the energy constraint where the processor's energy consumption is at most equal to the energy harvested in the storage associated to the processor. If the system feasibility is satisfied then the system operates normally. Besides, if at least one of the feasibility conditions is violated then the dynamic software reconfiguration solutions are applied one by one in order to reconfigure the system and re-establish the system feasibility. We decompose the scheduling problem into two phases:

• Static phase executed offline where the energy predictor algorithm is applied to extrapolate information about the harvested energy in the future. Based on this estimation, it builds the execution windows. Then, the task allocation algorithm is applied, • Dynamic phase executed online in subsystems, in order to modify the real-time execution of the task allocations from the previous phase to adapt to unpredictable fluctuation in energy availability and to cope with unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios. In the following sections, we describe in details the proposed approach.

div.head: B. Task Assignment Heuristic
div.p: The static task allocation problem is divided into two steps. The first one is the assignment of the critical task set. The main objective for the first step is to guarantee that all the critical tasks will respect their hard deadlines in the different execution windows. The second step aims to assign the non-critical tasks. The objective of the second step is to reduce the miss deadline ratio of the non criticaltask set. The following steps describe the basic idea of our task allocation heuristic:

Step 1: Sort the set of critical tasks in a decreasing order of degree of criticity dc i , Step 2: Assign task τ i to processor P j where the real-time and energy constraints are satisfied, Step 3: Assign the set of non-critical tasks to the set of processors.
The energy harvesting task assignment heuristic is depicted in Algorithm 1.

div.head: C. Dynamic Adjustment Algorithm
div.p: The dynamic adjustment algorithm is performed in two cases i) A dynamic reconfiguration scenario applied at runtime that evolves the system towards an infeasible state, ii) The margin error calculated in the beginning of each execution window exceeds some predefined thresholds E r . The dynamic adjustment algorithm performs three functions: i) Migration migrate critical or non-critical tasks from one processor to another one, iii) Degradation of execution mode of non-critical tasks Degrade the quality of service where non-critical tasks may be executed according to (m,k)-firm constraints, and ii) Removal of non-critical tasks Delete noncritical tasks so as to minimize the global deadline miss ratio. The three functions are performed in a hierarchical order. The energy harvesting dynamic adjustment algorithm is depicted in Algorithm 2.

1) Migration Solution: This solution proposes to migrate a task from a faulty processor to a non faulty one. Hence, the solution is performed in two steps: The first step selects the task or the tasks to be migrated. The second step selects the processor where the tasks will be affected.

In this case, the tasks may be executed under a (m,k)-firm constraint according to user requirements which indicate that the deadlines of at least m among any k consecutive instances of a task must be met. div.head: VI. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: We explore the performance of the proposed algorithms in the presence of the variable solar based energy harvesting. In order to evaluate this approach, we consider a set of 50 tasks to be schedulable on three heterogeneous processors. We assume a set of unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios applied repeatedly. The periodicity of a reconfiguration is equal to 1000 time units. Each scenario adds a set of n tasks such that n is randomly chosen between 10 and 50. The period of each task is chosen randomly between 10 and 100. The WCET is randomly chosen between 6 and 20. We have run several sets of simulations to investigate the performance of i) The energy harvesting prediction algorithm, ii) The task assignment algorithm, and iii) The dynamic adjustment algorithm. In order to evaluate the performance of our energy harvesting prediction algorithm, we assume that the interval I is equal to a day. In this experimentation, we consider measurement data in 7 consecutive days collected through PVP SM50-H (Siemens) [23]. The estimation interval I starts from 7am and ends at 5pm that presents sunrise and sunset in the area of Tunisia in the month of December. The prediction interval I is discretized into a set of equal duration time slots such that each one is equal to one hour. We present in the following two days predictions. Figure. that the proposed solar energy predictor algorithm presents high performance in term of prediction. Furthermore, the provided prediction follows the main shapes of the real energy values. The performance evaluation of the proposed task assignment and dynamic adjustment algorithm concerns the miss ratio deadline of non-critical tasks with guarantee that all critical tasks meet their hard deadlines. The success ratio of the set of critical tasks is measured for both the static allocation with and without the dynamic adjustment. Figure . 5 clearly shows the significant success ratio improvement of critical tasks by implementing the dynamic adjustment algorithm with the three proposed solutions (up to 85% when the system utilization is equal to three). Figure . 6 presents the success ratio of non-critical tasks by implementing both the static allocation with and without dynamic adjustment. It can be derived from this figure that the success ratio achieves 35% when the system utilization is equal to three by applying the dynamic adjustment algorithm and the proposed three solutions. In order to evaluate the impact of the energy harvesting prediction algorithm on deadline success, the percentage of satisfied deadlines of the same tasks set is measured for the three proposed solutions in Figure. It clearly shows that the performance of all algorithms degrades when the processor utilization factor increases due to a set of reconfiguration scenarios applied repeatedly at run-time. The removal tasks solution has the strongest degradation. Indeed, when U exceeds 1.34, the migration solution outperforms all other solutions. Figure . 8 presents the percentage of satisfied deadlines when we apply the migration, degradation, and removal of tasks in the presence of the energy harvesting prediction algorithm. In general, migration outperforms all other solutions. By comparing these two figures, we can derive that the energy harvesting prediction algorithm increases the accuracy of our proposed solutions. Further, the percentage of satisfied deadlines for utilization factor equals to three, is equal to 49.4%, whereas it is equal to 64.8% in the presence of the energy harvesting prediction algorithm.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, the task scheduling problem for reconfigurable real-time distributed embedded systems powered by renewable energy has been considered. The objective is to guarantee that all critical tasks succeded their hard deadlines, and minimize the miss deadline ratio of non critical ones. We have proposed a solution with a two-stage algorithm i) A static one for task assignment based on energy prediction and, ii) A dynamic adjustment one to maintain schedulability of the application software. Extensive simulation experi-ments show that the proposed approach achieves the deadline success ratio up to 85% for the set of critical tasks and up to 35% for the set of non-critical tasks when the system utilization is equal to three. The energy harvesting prediction algorithm increases the accuracy of our proposed solutions. Further, the percentage of satisfied deadlines for utilization factor equals to three, is equal to 49.4%, whereas it is equal to 64.8% in the presence of the energy harvesting prediction algorithm.

In a future work, we plan to extend our model in order to integrate the communication issue. The messages are characterized by deadlines and energy requirements for their transmission. The energy neutrality of the global system imposes to identify and evaluate new scheduling techniques for messages which are adapted to energy harvesting distributed systems.
